newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul summons Kim's aide, opposition MP over Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: Seoul summons Kim's aide, opposition MP over Hanbo.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors summoned three politicians, including a close associate of President Kim Young-sam, for questioning on Monday over huge loans to the failed Hanbo Steel Co, a prosecution official said.

Widening their probe into a loan scandal that has shocked South Korea and put the heat on Kim in a presidential election year, prosecutors said they wanted to determine if politicians pressured bankers into extending loans to Hanbo Steel.
"Prosecutors will focus their investigation on whether there were political pressures on bankers or kickbacks involved," a prosecution official told Reuters.
He said three members of parliament, including Hong In-gil, a senior official at the presidential Blue House until last year, were asked to appear at the prosecution office on Monday.
Also summoned by prosecutors were Kwon Roh-kap, a senior aide to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, and Chung Jae-chull, a leading member of the ruling New Korea Party.
"Mr Chung Jae-chull and Mr Hong In-gil are now being questioned by prosecutors," the official said. Kwon told prosecutors he would report to them on Tuesday.

They were the first politicians to be probed over loans totalling five trillion won ($5.8 billion) provided to Hanbo Steel, South Korea's second largest steelmaker, before it was declared insolvent on January 23.
President Kim last month ordered a probe into loans. He has called the scandal a typical example of corruption.
Prosecutors have already arrested Chung Tae-soo, founder of the Hanbo Group and its steelmaking flagship, and two leading bankers over the loan scandal.
Hong, who has been President Kim's close associate for more than two decades, has denied taking money from Hanbo.

Kwon, a leading member of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, said he had nothing to do with Hanbo loans. But he said last week he had accepted between 150 million and 160 million won ($173,000-184,000) from the Hanbo founder, partly to fund an election campaign.
The other lawmaker has not publicly commented.

Opposition parties have accused the government of peddling influence for the huge loans that allowed Hanbo to emerge as South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate by rapidly expanding its steelmaking flagship and by acquiring or setting up 18 firms over the past three years.
Hanbo's founder has been charged with fraud and other violations while the two bankers were accused of taking 400 million won each from him in return for offering loans to Hanbo.
State radio said about half a dozen other politicians, including some tipped as contenders in December's presidential polls, were due to be summoned by the prosecutors.
Prosecutors declined to confirm the radio report.
Political analysts said the Hanbo scandal could have a major impact on the presidential elections.

"President Kim's image has been badly damaged recently," Cho Chang-hyun, political science professor at Hanyang University said. "Unless the probe into Hanbo loans produces a convincing outcome, the president's morality would be questioned and the prospects for the ruling camp would be dismal."
President Kim is barred from seeking re-election, but analysts expect him to seek to install a protege.

The president gave top priority to rooting out corruption after he took office in 1993, but his anti-graft drive has been hurt in the past year following the arrest of several of his top officials, including a defence minister, on bribery charges.
